What to Expect in a First Counselling Session
A simple overview of what usually happens when someone begins counselling.

Starting counselling can feel like a big step, especially if you are not sure what will happen in the first appointment. A first session is usually a gentle beginning rather than a test or interview you need to prepare for perfectly.

Your counsellor may ask what brings you in, what you hope to get from counselling, and what support has or has not helped before. You can share at your own pace. You are also welcome to ask questions about confidentiality, fees, scheduling, and the counsellor's approach.

By the end of the first session, you should have a clearer sense of whether the fit feels right and what next steps might look like.

Support for worry, panic, perfectionism, stress, and the body signals that can make life feel smaller.

Anxiety can show up as racing thoughts, tension, avoidance, irritability, panic, or a constant sense that something is about to go wrong. Counselling offers space to understand what your nervous system is trying to protect you from and to build steadier ways of responding.

In this work, we may explore patterns in thoughts and behaviour, develop grounding tools, and look at the experiences that shaped your current responses. The goal is not to erase anxiety completely, but to help you feel more choice, confidence, and room to live.

Counselling for low mood, numbness, self-criticism, burnout, and feeling disconnected from yourself or others.

Depression can make everyday tasks feel heavy and can affect sleep, motivation, concentration, relationships, and self-worth. Counselling can help you name what has been happening without shame and begin rebuilding support one manageable step at a time.

Together, you might look at cycles of withdrawal, old beliefs about yourself, grief, stress, or nervous system exhaustion. The pace should feel collaborative and respectful of your capacity.

Support for communication, boundaries, attachment patterns, conflict, and feeling more connected in important relationships.

Relationships can bring both comfort and strain. Counselling can help you notice repeated patterns, understand emotional reactions, and practise clearer communication and boundaries.

This work may focus on family dynamics, dating, partnership, friendship, workplace relationships, or the way earlier experiences shape current connection. The aim is to support more honesty, self-respect, and care in how you relate to yourself and others.
